name: Petpooja
tagline: Restaurant billing and POS software for Indian outlets, with KOT printing, inventory, GST bills and delivery aggregator integration.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: You can absolutely build a till: menu, table, order, bill, print. What you cannot build in a session is the part restaurants actually buy, which is the pipe into Swiggy and Zomato so online orders land in the same kitchen queue as walk-ins without someone retyping them off a tablet. Add GST-compliant invoice formats, thermal printer and cash drawer quirks, offline-first behaviour when the wifi dies mid dinner rush, and a support line that answers at 11pm on a Saturday. A personal build is fine if you run one tiny counter and take no online orders. If you take online orders, the DIY version is a second job.
coreLoopDIY: A local-only touch POS that takes dine-in and counter orders, prints KOTs and a GST-style bill to a thermal printer, and closes the day with a sales summary.
requirements: A machine on site that stays on, laptop or mini PC
ESC/POS thermal printer reachable over LAN or USB
A tablet or touchscreen for the order screen
Someone technical on call when the printer stops printing
whatYouLose: Swiggy and Zomato order ingestion, menu sync and item toggling from one screen
Payment terminal and UPI reconciliation that matches the bill automatically
GST invoice formats and e-invoice handling that an accountant will accept without argument
Multi-outlet reporting, stock consumption mapping and vendor purchase flows
Support staff who fix your billing machine during service instead of you debugging it
moatNotes: Aggregator APIs are gated business relationships, not public endpoints. That alone ends most DIY POS ambitions.
whyPeopleStillPay: A restaurant POS is not software people admire, it is software that must not fail while forty people are waiting for food. Petpooja is paid for because it already speaks to the delivery aggregators, the printers, the payment terminals and the tax formats, and because when something breaks the owner calls a number instead of opening a terminal. The per outlet cost is small against one botched dinner service, so the build-versus-buy math almost never favours building.
notes: The till is a weekend, the ecosystem is not. The moat is the aggregator integrations, the tax formats and the hardware certification, none of which you can get by writing code alone.
prompt:
Build a local-first restaurant POS for a single small outlet. No cloud, no accounts, no telemetry.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js (App Router) with TypeScript, run in dev or as a local production build
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, single file db at ./data/pos.db
- Tailwind for UI, designed for a 10 inch touchscreen: big tap targets, no hover-only controls
- node-thermal-printer for ESC/POS output over network or USB

Data model: categories, items (name, price, tax rate, veg flag, active flag), tables, orders, order_items, payments, day_closures.

Features in scope:
1. Order screen: pick a table or Counter, tap items into a running cart, adjust quantity, add a free-text note per line, void a line with a reason.
2. Kitchen ticket: print a KOT to the configured printer showing only new-since-last-print lines, so reprints do not duplicate work.
3. Bill: itemised total, per-item tax breakdown computed from the item tax rate, optional flat discount, rounded grand total, printed on the same printer.
4. Payment: mark bill as Cash, Card or UPI, record amount, close the order, free the table.
5. Menu admin page: CRUD for categories and items, toggle item availability.
6. Day close: a page that sums today's orders by payment mode, shows voids and discounts, writes a day_closures row, and exports a CSV to ./exports.
7. Offline sanity: every write hits SQLite synchronously, the app must work with the network cable pulled as long as the printer is reachable; if printing fails, queue the job and show a retry button, never lose the order.

Out of scope, do not attempt or stub: Swiggy or Zomato integration, online payment gateways, e-invoicing, multi-outlet sync, inventory depletion, staff payroll, customer loyalty.

Config: printer host, port and interface type in .env, plus outlet name, GSTIN string and address used on the bill header. Ship a .env.example.

Seed a demo menu of 20 items across 4 categories and 8 tables. Include a README with one command to start, one to back up the db file, and a printer troubleshooting section. Write the printing layer behind an interface with a console-printer implementation so the whole thing is testable without hardware.
